proof:
# Three homothetic fibers: all scale ratios and translations

Let d>=2 and let K be any full-dimensional compact convex body in R^d with centroid zero and volume V. Consider an actual convex mixed-integer source with its three positive fibers at bases -1,0,1:

    A=a+rK,       B=b+RK,       C=c+sK,

where r,R,s>0. Assume the actual midpoint inclusion `(A+C)/2 subset B`; there are no other positive-volume integer fibers. Then an actual mixed-integer point has every closed containing ambient halfspace of mass at least

    (Gamma_d/2) V(r^d+R^d+s^d),
    Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.                              (1)

No symmetry of K, nesting of the original fibers, or affinity of their three original centroids is assumed. The endpoint radii can have any ratio. This is a three-fiber theorem; it does not assert the unrestricted mixed-integer conjecture.

A deterministic selection suffices: if a fiber has at least half the total mass, use its ordinary centroid. Otherwise use the ordinary centroid of the middle fiber B.

The only previous functional input beyond ordinary Grünbaum is the proved measurable-subset inequality in `candidate dafd411c026c302c`, Section 6. Its geometric use is restated below. The new point is that in the remaining nonnested radius strip the extra middle volume contributes at the SAME centroid, compensating for trimming the small endpoint.

## 1. Normalize translations and identify all remaining cases

Reverse the integer base if needed so that r<=s. Apply the permitted affine shear

    (z,x) -> (z,x-b-z(c-b)).

It preserves integer bases, all fiber volumes, and the class of all ambient halfspaces. In the new coordinates,

    B=RK,       C=sK,       A=a'+rK,
    a'=a+c-2b.

The midpoint inclusion and support functions give

    a'+(r+s)K subset 2RK,
    a' in (2R-r-s)K.                                  (2)

The coefficient `2R-r-s` is nonnegative: ordinary Brunn–Minkowski applied to the midpoint inclusion gives `2R>=r+s`. When it is zero, (2) means `a'=0`. For positive coefficient, (2) follows from `u.a'<=(2R-r-s)h_K(u)` for every u. In particular

    A subset (2R-s)K.                                 (3)

Since the centroid zero is interior to K, nonnegative dilations are nested. If R<=s, (3) gives the actual nested chain

    A subset RK subset sK.                            (4)

This is already covered by the archived nested-three-fiber theorem. For completeness, an explicit version is given in Section 4 below.

If `R^d>=r^d+s^d`, the middle centroid alone pays (1) by ordinary Grünbaum. Therefore the only new case is

    r<=s<R,       R^d<r^d+s^d.                        (5)

Write `epsilon=R-s>0`. In this case

    2 epsilon<r.                                      (6)

Indeed for d>=2 and s>=r>0,

    (s+r/2)^d-s^d >= (r+r/2)^d-r^d
                         =r^d[(3/2)^d-1]>r^d.

The first inequality follows because `(x+r/2)^d-x^d` increases in x. Thus `R>=s+r/2` would contradict (5).

## 2. A translated inner copy of the small endpoint

Put `alpha=s+2 epsilon-r=2R-s-r>=0`. From (2), `a' in alpha K`. The body

    A_0=a'+(r-2 epsilon)K                              (7)

is contained in both A and sK. Containment in A follows from (6) and nested dilations about zero. For containment in sK, write `a'=alpha k_0` when alpha>0 and use

    alpha+(r-2 epsilon)=s,

so convexity gives `alpha k_0+(r-2 epsilon)K subset sK`. The case alpha=0 follows directly. Its exact volume is

    a_0=(r-2 epsilon)^d V.                             (8)

This is an actual convex subbody of the small endpoint, with its original translation retained. Its centroid need not be zero.

## 3. A sharp scalar trimming inequality

For every integer d>=2, every s>=r>0, and `0<=epsilon<=r/2`,

    (r-2 epsilon)^d
       >= (1/2)[r^d+s^d-(s+epsilon)^d].               (9)

The right side is allowed to be negative. The coefficient 1/2 is sharp simultaneously over these parameters: equality occurs for d=2, s=r, epsilon=r/3.

To prove (9), set `lambda=s/r>=1` and `t=epsilon/r in[0,1/2]`. For fixed t, the difference `(lambda+t)^d-lambda^d` is increasing in lambda, so it suffices to prove

    2(1-2t)^d+(1+t)^d>=2.                             (10)

Let `m=d-1>=1` and `k=4^(-1/m)`. The derivative of the left side vanishes exactly when

    1-2t=k(1+t),       t=(1-k)/(2+k).

The left side is convex on `[0,1/2]`, and this point is in that interval. Its exact minimum is

    3^d/[2(2+k)^(d-1)].                               (11)

Convexity of the power `x^m` gives

    ((2+k)/3)^m <= (2+k^m)/3 = 3/4.

Therefore `(2+k)^(d-1)<=3^d/4`, and (11) is at least 2. For d=2 the minimum is exactly 2 at t=1/3, proving the stated sharpness. For d>2 the power inequality is strict because k<1.

Under (5), the bracket in (9) is positive. Since `Gamma_d<=1/2`, we obtain the required form

    a_0 >= Gamma_d V(r^d+s^d-R^d).                   (12)

## 4. All original caps at one actual point

Recall the proved subset inequality: for a full-dimensional convex body L with centroid zero and a measurable subset E of mass e, the three sources E,L,L at bases -1,0,1 have every nonvertical cap through `(0,0)` of mass at least

    Gamma_d |L|+e/2.                                 (13)

The endpoint thresholds are opposite and the middle threshold is zero. The set E need not have centroid zero. Closed cut boundaries have zero d-volume, also for E by domination.

In the strip (5), apply (13) to the actual copies `A_0,sK,sK` contained respectively in A,B,C. For any fixed nonzero continuous normal u, the extra middle cap is EXACTLY

    |RK intersect {u.x>=0}|-|sK intersect {u.x>=0}|
      =(R^d-s^d)|K intersect {u.x>=0}|
      >=Gamma_d (R^d-s^d)V.                          (14)

This exact same-center homothetic identity is the necessary extra payment. We have not assigned a generic Grünbaum contribution to an arbitrary enlarged body at an unrelated point.

Equations (13)–(14) prove the all-cap lower bound

    cap mass >= Gamma_d R^d V+a_0/2.                 (15)

Purely base-normal through-point caps contain the whole middle fiber and at least the smaller endpoint mass, hence have mass at least `(R^d+r^d)V`; this also exceeds (15). Every containing cap contains a parallel through-point cap. Thus (15) applies to every original closed containing halfspace at the actual middle centroid.

By (12), the right side of (15) is at least the target (1). In fact (9) supplies the quantitative surplus

    cap mass - (Gamma_d/2)V(r^d+R^d+s^d)
      >= ((1-2Gamma_d)/4)V(r^d+s^d-R^d)>0             (16)

throughout the strictly nonheavy strip for d>=2.

To complete the other nonheavy case R<=s without invoking the full nested theorem, use (4) and apply (13) to `A,RK,RK`, retaining the second RK inside C. This pays `Gamma_d R^d V+r^dV/2` at the middle centroid. If the largest endpoint is not heavy, `s^d<R^d+r^d`, this amount is at least (1), because

    Gamma_d(s^d+r^d-R^d)<=2Gamma_d r^d<=r^d.

Vertical caps again contain the whole middle plus a whole endpoint. If instead `s^d>=R^d+r^d`, the centroid of C is a heavy-fiber solution. Together with the heavy middle case this exhausts every allowed positive radius triple and proves the deterministic selection rule.

## 5. Scope and dimension one

The proof uses homothety of the middle and the larger endpoint precisely in (14), after centering both by one allowed shear. It covers arbitrary original translations, arbitrary positive scale ratios, and arbitrary common body K. It makes no claim for an arbitrary nonhomothetic middle body; the separate ratio theorem `candidate 7e2883b5a7576b2b` has that different scope.

For d=1, all three fibers are intervals and the full three-interval statement is already proved in `candidate 5048c7e97ca98aef`, including all translations and oblique slopes. The new trimming argument is stated for d>=2; its scalar estimate is false in general for d=1 and is not imported into that case.

The exact verifier `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_three_homothetic_all_ratios.py` checks the scalar inequality, sharp equality, compatibility coefficients, cap-payment arithmetic and quantitative surplus on rational radius triples. The proof above, rather than a finite screen, establishes the all-parameter theorem.
